one_liner: In-process software sandbox for native Arm64/x86-64 code; about 7% overhead versus 16-67% for AOT Wasm engines on SPEC 2017.
what_it_does: LFI isolates untrusted native code (C, C++, hand-written assembly) inside a 4 GiB region of the host process, much as WebAssembly or Native Client do, but without a bytecode: you recompile the code with the LFI Clang toolchain into an ELF, and the runtime (liblfi, or the lfi-run command-line loader) verifies the machine code and runs it. Host code drives sandboxes through a C API (lfi_new, lfi_box_new, lfi_ctx_run, lfi_box_mapat, copy-in/copy-out helpers), and lfi-bind generates trampolines so a host can call functions of a sandboxed static library directly. It is not a Wasm VM and cannot run .wasm modules; it replaces Wasm as the isolation mechanism when you control the source build.
how_it_is_fast: Software fault isolation with guard-free addressing: on Arm64 every load/store is rewritten into the 32-bit zero-extending register addressing mode off a reserved base register (x21), so most memory accesses cost 0-1 extra cycles instead of a separate 2-cycle guard; stack-pointer and link-register invariants, redundant-guard hoisting into two reserved registers and 80 KiB guard regions remove most remaining checks. Because the rewrite runs on the assembly that a normal optimising LLVM pipeline emits, the code keeps full -O3 + LTO optimisation (no extra Wasm IR or C translation step, no Wasm indirect-call type checks), and a small static verifier rather than the compiler carries the trust. Host calls and cross-sandbox yields go through a read-only call table without a hardware mode switch (22-26 ns syscall vs 129-160 ns native Linux, 17-18 ns yield in the paper).
when_to_use: You need to isolate an existing C/C++ library (parsers, codecs, compression, image decoders) inside your own process and can rebuild it from source with a dedicated toolchain.
Throughput-sensitive sandboxed code on Linux Arm64 or x86-64 where 15-70% Wasm AOT overhead is too much and about 7% (full isolation) or 1.5-5% (stores-only fault isolation) is acceptable.
Many sandboxes per process with very frequent host/sandbox transitions: up to about 64K sandboxes on Arm64 (about 3K on x86-64), tens-of-cycles context switches.
Code that uses features WASI cannot express: C++ exceptions, setjmp/longjmp, hand-written assembly, threads, fork-style process emulation.
Research or prototyping of SFI-based compartmentalisation (for example RLBox-style library sandboxing) where you can follow an active research codebase.
when_not_to_use: You need portable, architecture-independent modules or a stable binary format: LFI binaries are tied to the target ISA and LFI toolchain version, by design.

You must run fully adversarial code today: the lfi-runtime README says the runtime is currently used for library isolation of code written by an honest party in SYS_MINIMAL mode, hardening for arbitrarily malicious programs is ongoing, and a sandbox can still make the runtime fault or abort.
Platforms other than Linux on Arm64/x86-64 (RISC-V is experimental; no Windows or macOS host runtime documented), or sandboxes that need more than 4 GiB of memory.
You only have third-party binaries or .wasm modules and cannot recompile: LFI needs source (or assembly) built with its toolchain and sysroot (musl, libc++, compiler-rt, mimalloc).

Production use that needs a stable API: the project restructured into separate repositories (lfi-runtime, lfi-rewriter, lfi-verifier, lfi-bind) in January 2026 and the library-sandboxing tutorial is still 'coming soon'.

integration.dependencies: LFI LLVM/Clang toolchain and LFI sysroot (musl, libc++, compiler-rt, mimalloc; prebuilt bundles on the releases page) for guest code; liblfi runtime built with meson/ninja; lfi-bind (Go) for library trampolines
integration.min_toolchain: Guest code: LFI-patched Clang (research release shipped LLVM 19; lfi-bench numbers use LLVM 20.1.7; paper used LLVM 15.0.7). Host runtime: C compiler plus meson and ninja; C++ for the optional sbox tainting library.
integration.platforms: Linux on Arm64 (ARMv8.0-A plus LSE) and x86-64; RISC-V experimental; tested on Apple M1/M2 under Asahi Linux (16 KiB pages), GCP T2A, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X
integration.thread_safety: Multithreaded sandboxes supported (one LFIContext per sandbox thread, per-thread alternate signal stack); per-box mapping/copy calls are synchronised by a per-box lock, but lfi_box_free must not run concurrently with other calls on the same box.

gotchas: Security defaults: lfi-run skips verification unless passed -v and gives the sandbox full filesystem access by default; LFIOptions also exposes no_verify and allow_wx, and liblfi does not stop a runtime from granting MAP_SHARED mappings that alias W and X pages. The lfi-llvm-toolchain README also says the upstream-LLVM aarch64_lfi target does not yet rewrite memory accesses or control flow, so build guests with the bundled rewriter toolchain and keep the verifier on.

x86-64 toolchain correctness bug, open issue #14 (filed 2026-10-06): at -O1/-O2 the TLS rewrite of 'cmpq %fs:var, %reg' uses the live source register as scratch, giving wrong results and crashes (for example in Rust std thread-local destructor lists); workaround -mno-tls-direct-seg-refs. This affects x86-64 guests, not the Arm64 numbers in the paper.

The paper's Wasm comparison is favourable to Wasm in some respects and unusual in others: WAMR and the authors' modified Wasm2c are non-conforming (no trap-semantics compiler barrier), the pinned-heap-register Wasm2c does not fully handle cross-module indirect calls, native code is run inside the LFI runtime so both sides share its faster syscalls, and only 7 of 14 benchmarks build for WASI. Table 4's LFI row (7.3% T2A / 6.4% M1) is identical to the paper's 14-benchmark geomean although the caption says it covers the 7-benchmark subset; the paper does not say whether it was recomputed.

On the artifact's open CoreMark alternative the gap is much smaller than on SPEC: LFI 1.10x native vs WAMR 1.13x, Wasm2c 1.16x and Wasmtime 2.66x (M1, Asahi Linux). Current SPEC configs run a single iteration per benchmark (iterations = 1, reportable = 0) with patched SPEC sources and integrity checks disabled, so per-benchmark differences of 1-2% are within noise.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LFI over wasm2c (WABT), WAMR or aWsm when you recompile C/C++ from source anyway, run on Linux Arm64/x86-64, and want the lowest in-process sandboxing overhead plus native features (exceptions, assembly, threads); pick wasm2c, w2c2 or WAMR when you need a portable Wasm module format, non-Linux hosts, or a spec-conforming, production-hardened runtime.
verified_claims_summary: In the ASPLOS 2024 paper, LFI-sandboxed SPEC CPU2017 rate benchmarks (LLVM 15.0.7 with LTO for native and LFI, Arm64 only; the repo's current SPEC configs use -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -static-pie -flto=full, and wasi-sdk clang -O3 -msimd128 -flto=full for Wasm) ran with 6.4% (Apple M1) and 7.3% (GCP T2A) geomean overhead over native LTO code, versus 18.2%/22.3% for WAMR 1.2.2 AOT, 15.7%/16.5% for a tuned Wasm2c 1.0.33 and 67.1%/47.0% for Wasmtime 16.0.0 AOT on the 7 benchmarks that build for WASI (about 1.11-1.14x faster than WAMR, derived from page data). The project's later lfi-bench SPEC runs with LLVM 20.1.7 + LTO report 6.9% on a Mac Mini M2 and 7.1% (AMD Ryzen 9 7950X) / 7.9% (unnamed Intel CPU) on x86-64 for full isolation, which back the HEAD README's 7%/8% figures.
status_note: Active research project (lfi-project/lfi last commit 2026-01-27, lfi-runtime 400+ commits, 119 stars on the umbrella repo), MIT-licensed at HEAD (the lfi-research branch with the paper's code is MPL-2.0); usable today for library isolation of trusted-but-buggy code, but the runtime is not yet hardened against fully malicious guests and the x86-64 toolchain has an open miscompilation.
